title: From Adam to Noah: Death and Hope
summary: Seth’s line carries God’s image and promise through ten generations, ruled by death, broken by Enoch’s translation, and closing in hope with Noah.
historicalContext: Genesis 5 spans the centuries between creation and the flood, about 1,656 years when the ages in the Hebrew text are added in sequence. The ages are given as real lifespans of real men: precise, varied, and far more restrained than the reigns of tens of thousands of years claimed for early kings in Mesopotamian lists. Humanity still lived close to its origin, with a vigor that had not yet run down, and God’s patience held back the full weight of the sentence of death. One result is striking: Adam was still alive when Lamech, Noah’s father, was born, so the account of creation, the fall, and the promise of the woman’s Seed could pass by living memory almost to the eve of the flood. Moses gave this record to Israel as the bridge joining their own ancestry to the first man God made.
literaryContext: The chapter opens the second “generations” section of Genesis (2:4; 5:1) and answers the brief notice of Seth and Enos in 4:25–26. It stands directly against Cain’s line in 4:17–24, which is listed without ages and ends in Lamech’s boast of vengeance. Ten paragraphs follow one fixed pattern: a man lives, fathers a named son, lives on and has sons and daughters, and dies. The repetition is the message, since death closes eight of the ten entries. Three departures stand out against the pattern: the opening that recalls the image of God, the seventh entry where Enoch walks with God and is taken, and the tenth where Lamech names Noah in hope of relief from the curse. Noah’s entry is left open until 9:28–29, so the flood account that follows reads as the continuation of this family record.
themes: The image of God carried through a fallen race
Death’s reign as the fulfilment of God’s word
Grace preserving the line of the promised Seed
Walking with God in an ungodly age
Translation as a pledge of victory over death
Longing for rest from the curse

outline.title: Creation Recalled
outline.summary: The record of Adam’s line opens by recalling that God made humanity, male and female, in His likeness, blessed them, and named them.

outline.title: Adam: Image Passed On, Death Fulfilled
outline.summary: Adam fathers Seth in his own likeness and, after 930 years, dies as God had warned.

outline.title: Seth to Jared: The Line Continues
outline.summary: Five generations follow the same pattern of birth, fatherhood, long life, and death, keeping the line of promise unbroken.

outline.title: Enoch Walks with God
outline.summary: The seventh from Adam lives in close fellowship with God and is taken without seeing death.

outline.title: Methuselah, Lamech, and Noah
outline.summary: The longest life ends near the flood, Lamech names Noah in hope of relief from the curse, and Noah’s three sons are named.

verses.bibleText: This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, in the likeness of God made he him;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“This is the book of the generations of Adam” marks a fresh beginning in Genesis. The heading echoes 2:4, where the generations of the heavens and the earth were introduced, and it is the only such heading in the book described as a “book,” a written record. Cain’s descendants were listed in 4:17–24 without any ages or years; now the line through which the promise will run receives a full, dated account. The difference in treatment is itself a statement about which family history matters for the purpose of God.

Before tracing a single descendant, the verse goes back to the source: “In the day that God created man.” Every other genealogy in Scripture begins with someone who was born. This one begins with a man who was made. Adam had no father but God, which is why Luke, reading the line from the other end, closes his genealogy of Jesus with the words “which was the son of God” (Luke 3:38). The human story is anchored in a deliberate act of the Creator, not in an unknown past.

“In the likeness of God made he him” repeats the dignity of Genesis 1:26–27 at a point where the narrative has already shown disobedience, expulsion from the garden, and a brother’s murder. The repetition is pointed. Sin had marred humanity, yet it had not cancelled what God made humans to be. Later Scripture still treats every person as bearing God’s likeness (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9), and that conviction stands at the head of a record dominated by death.

The Greek Old Testament renders the heading with the phrase that opens Matthew’s Gospel: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ” (Matthew 1:1). The first book of generations follows the descendants of a created man into the grave. The second traces the ancestry of the Son, who is Himself “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15) and in whom the likeness lost in Adam is restored.

wordNotes.term: סֵפֶר תּוֹלְדֹת אָדָם (sefer toledot ’adam) — the book of the generations of Adam
wordNotes.explanation: Sefer refers to any written document, whether a scroll, a tablet, or even a short legal deed such as a bill of divorce. Toledot comes from the verb for begetting and denotes what was produced from someone, here Adam’s descendants. In Genesis the formula introduces the account that follows rather than summarizing what precedes. The Greek translation, biblos geneseōs, is the phrase Matthew uses to open his record of Jesus’ ancestry.

wordNotes.term: בִּדְמוּת אֱלֹהִים (bidmut ’elohim) — in the likeness of God
wordNotes.explanation: Genesis 1:26 used two terms, image and likeness; this summary uses only demut, likeness, which stresses resemblance or correspondence. The two words overlap in meaning and should not be pressed into separate parts of human nature. The point is that humanity was made to reflect its Maker, and the next verse shows that likeness being carried forward.

verses.bibleText: Male and female created he them; and blessed them, and called their name Adam, in the day when they were created.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Male and female created he them” returns to the wording of Genesis 1:27. Humanity bears God’s likeness as man and woman together, and the whole genealogy that follows depends on that pairing. Although the list will name only fathers and their chosen sons, the introduction refuses to let the reader forget that both the man and the woman came from God’s hand and both stand under His approval.

“And blessed them” recalls the blessing of 1:28, which centered on fruitfulness and filling the earth. The chapter becomes the record of that blessing at work. Each entry repeats that a patriarch “begat sons and daughters,” so that the curse spoken in chapter 3 is seen running alongside, and never cancelling, the blessing spoken in chapter 1. Children were still being born in a world under judgment, and every birth testified that God had not abandoned His purpose for the race.

“And called their name Adam” adds something not stated in chapter 1. God Himself names humanity, and the name He gives belongs to both of them. Here ’adam carries its generic sense, mankind; from the next verse it serves as the personal name of the first man. To name is to exercise authority and to express care, as God named the day and the night, and later His people (Isaiah 43:1). That the man and woman share one God-given name underlines their common nature and equal dignity, the same truth Peter expresses when he calls husband and wife “heirs together of the grace of life” (1 Peter 3:7).

The verse closes as it began, “in the day when they were created.” Jesus appealed to this same creation pattern when He spoke of marriage: “from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female” (Mark 10:6). The order established at the beginning still served as the standard in His teaching.

wordNotes.term: זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה (zakhar uneqevah) — male and female
wordNotes.explanation: These are the ordinary Hebrew terms for the two sexes, used also of animals entering the ark. Applied to humanity in creation, the pairing affirms that both sexes equally bear God’s likeness and together receive His blessing. Jesus quotes the phrase from the Greek Old Testament when He grounds marriage in the order of creation.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקְרָא אֶת־שְׁמָם אָדָם (vayyiqra’ ’et-shemam ’adam) — and called their name Adam
wordNotes.explanation: The plural “their name” shows that ’adam is here the name of the race, inclusive of man and woman, before it becomes the personal name of the first man in verse 3. In Genesis, naming expresses authority and relationship: God names light and darkness, Adam names the animals, and here the Creator names the creatures made in His likeness.

verses.bibleText: And Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image; and called his name Seth:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With “Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son,” the pattern of the chapter begins. Seth was not Adam’s firstborn. Cain and Abel came before him, and other children may also have been born in those years. The genealogy is not tracing eldest sons; it follows the son through whom the line of promise would continue. Eve had recognized this when she named him, saying that God had “appointed me another seed instead of Abel” (4:25). The hope of the woman’s Seed in 3:15 had seemed to die with Abel and to be disqualified in Cain. In Seth, God provided a new beginning.

The phrase “in his own likeness, after his image” deliberately echoes 1:26, though the two terms appear in reverse order. Adam passes on to his son what God had given him. The image of God continued in the human race after the fall, and every descendant of Adam shares it. That is why human life remains sacred in Genesis 9:6 and why cursing a person is condemned as cursing one made “after the similitude of God” (James 3:9).

Yet the wording has shifted. God made Adam “in the likeness of God” (5:1); Adam begets Seth “in his own likeness.” The son bears his father’s nature, and that nature is now a fallen one. Seth inherited both the dignity of the image and the mortality that entered through sin, as the next two verses make plain. David would later confess that he was shaped in iniquity from his first moment (Psalm 51:5), and Paul explains that through one man sin entered the world, “and death by sin” (Romans 5:12).

The New Testament gathers these threads in Christ, the last Adam. “As we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:49). What Adam could only pass on in a damaged form, Christ renews, as believers are remade “after the image of him that created him” (Colossians 3:10). The line that began with Seth was moving toward the One who would restore the likeness itself.

wordNotes.term: בִּדְמוּתוֹ כְּצַלְמוֹ (bidmuto ketsalmo) — in his own likeness, after his image
wordNotes.explanation: The two nouns of Genesis 1:26, tselem (image) and demut (likeness), reappear here in reverse order, a deliberate echo that ties Seth’s birth to the creation of humanity. The pronoun “his” refers to Adam. The image God gave is transmitted through ordinary birth, yet it is now received from a father who has sinned and must die.

wordNotes.term: שֵׁת (Shet) — Seth
wordNotes.explanation: Eve explains the name by the verb shit, “to set” or “appoint”: God had appointed another seed in place of Abel. The name speaks of replacement and divine provision rather than of any quality in the child. Seth heads the line that Luke traces upward to Adam and to God.

verses.bibleText: And the days of Adam after he had begotten Seth were eight hundred years: and he begat sons and daughters:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The days of Adam after he had begotten Seth were eight hundred years” introduces the second element of each entry, the long span of life after the named son is born. These are presented as actual years. Adam’s life stretched across most of the age before the flood, and the totals in this chapter show that he was still living when Lamech, Noah’s father, was born. The man who had walked in Eden, heard God’s voice, fallen, and received the first promise of redemption could tell that story in person to eight generations of his descendants. The knowledge of creation and of the coming Seed did not depend on distant rumor.

“And he begat sons and daughters” is the refrain that shows the blessing of 1:28 at work. Adam and Eve had many more children than the three Genesis names, and this explains where Cain found a wife (4:17) and how the earth began to fill so quickly (6:1). The unnamed sons and daughters were not insignificant to God; children remain “an heritage of the LORD” (Psalm 127:3). The record simply follows one thread out of a growing family, the thread on which the promise hung.

The verse also carries a note of sorrow. Adam lived eight centuries after Seth’s birth, long enough to watch the consequences of his own choice spread through his descendants, including the violence of Cain’s line. Long life in a fallen world meant long acquaintance with what sin had done.

wordNotes.term: בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת (banim uvanot) — sons and daughters
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase recurs in every entry of the chapter except Noah’s. It indicates further children beyond the one named, without implying that the named son was the firstborn. The constant mention of daughters prepares for 6:1, where the multiplying of daughters becomes the setting for the corruption that led to the flood.

verses.bibleText: And all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years: and he died.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years: and he died.” With these words the first man’s brief biography ends, and the refrain of the chapter is established. God had said, “in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die” (2:17). The serpent had contradicted Him: “Ye shall not surely die” (3:4). Adam’s death settles the question. The penalty was real, and the denial of it was the first lie. The process of dying began the day Adam sinned, when he was barred from the tree of life (3:22–24); the long delay before his death was mercy, not exemption.

The ages in this chapter are given with sober precision. They vary from man to man, they never reach a thousand years, and they are modest beside the fabulous reigns of tens of thousands of years claimed for early kings in other ancient lists. Attempts to turn them into dynasties, symbolic codes, or shorter units of time do not fit a text that records the age at fatherhood, the years that followed, and the total. They are best read as actual lifespans. Humanity had not long left the Creator’s hand, the vigor of creation had not yet run down, and God in patience held back the full stroke of the sentence. After the flood, lifespans fall steadily until they reach the measure Moses knew: “threescore years and ten” (Psalm 90:10).

What death meant for Adam is stated in God’s own words: “dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (3:19). The breath of life given in 2:7 was withdrawn, and the living person ceased to live. Genesis does not describe Adam’s conscious self departing to another place. Scripture consistently describes the dead as knowing nothing (Ecclesiastes 9:5) and as sleeping until God raises them (Daniel 12:2; John 11:11–14).

Paul looks at this chapter and concludes that “death reigned from Adam to Moses” (Romans 5:14). The refrain will sound eight times before the chapter ends. Its only answer lies in the second Adam: “as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

wordNotes.term: וַיָּמֹת (vayyamot) — and he died
wordNotes.explanation: This short verb closes eight of the ten entries in the chapter. It comes from the same root as the warning “thou shalt surely die” in 2:17, so each occurrence reads as the fulfilment of God’s word. The Hebrew uses it of the end of life, the return of the person to dust, with no suggestion of continued conscious existence elsewhere.

wordNotes.term: תְּשַׁע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וּשְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה (tesha‘ me’ot shanah ushloshim shanah) — nine hundred and thirty years
wordNotes.explanation: The chapter’s numbers have come down in three ancient forms: the Hebrew text, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Greek translation, which differ chiefly in the ages at fatherhood. The Hebrew text, which the King James Version follows, is the best-preserved witness, and its figures yield about 1,656 years from creation to the flood. The total lifespans are largely the same in all three.

verses.bibleText: And Seth lived an hundred and five years, and begat Enos:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Seth lived an hundred and five years, and begat Enos.” From this point the pattern set by Adam’s entry runs with very little variation. The plainness is deliberate. These men are remembered not for cities, inventions, or songs, as in Cain’s line (4:17–22), but simply for living, fathering the next link in the chain, and dying.

Enos has already appeared in 4:26, where his birth is joined to a notable development: “then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.” The Sethite family was marked by public worship of the true God. While Cain’s descendants built and boasted, this line prayed. Whatever else is unknown about Seth, he raised a household in which the name of the LORD was invoked.

The name Enos is itself a common Hebrew word for a human being, often used in passages that dwell on human weakness and brevity. Coming so soon after the name Adam, it may reflect a sober awareness of what humanity had become, though the text does not explain it. Either way, the son of Seth was born into a race that knew its need of God, and in that knowledge it began to call on Him.

wordNotes.term: אֱנוֹשׁ (’Enosh) — Enos
wordNotes.explanation: As a common noun ’enosh means “man” or “mankind,” much like ’adam. It frequently appears where Scripture reflects on human frailty, as in “What is man, that thou art mindful of him?” and “As for man, his days are as grass.” The word itself does not mean “weak,” but its usage often carries a sense of mortal limitation.

verses.bibleText: And Seth lived after he begat Enos eight hundred and seven years, and begat sons and daughters:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Seth lived another eight hundred and seven years after Enos was born, and “begat sons and daughters.” The family was multiplying generation upon generation, with fathers living alongside their great-great-grandchildren. Most of these descendants are never named. Scripture follows one thread, but the God who records the line knew every child born into it, and the growth of the family was His blessing in action.

Seth’s long life also meant long influence. A household that called on the name of the LORD had centuries in which to teach that worship to those who came after.

wordNotes.term: וַיּוֹלֶד (vayyoled) — and begat
wordNotes.explanation: This causative form of the verb “to bear” means “to father” and appears with unusual frequency in Genesis 5 and in the parallel list of 11:10–26. Combined with the age of the father at the birth, it presents a direct succession of fathers and sons, giving the chapter the character of a chronological record.

verses.bibleText: And all the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years: and he died.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years: and he died.” The refrain falls a second time, now on the man God appointed in Abel’s place. Seth belonged to the godly line and led a family that worshiped the LORD, yet piety did not exempt him from the sentence passed on Adam’s race. “It is appointed unto men once to die” (Hebrews 9:27).

Adding the figures shows that Seth outlived his father by more than a century and was still alive after Enoch had been taken. He saw the first translation of a human being and then went down to the dust himself. The hope of the faithful had to look beyond this life, to a resurrection that God would bring in His time.

wordNotes.term: שָׁנָה (shanah) — year
wordNotes.explanation: This is the ordinary Hebrew word for a solar year, the same unit God appointed the lights of the heavens to mark on the fourth day. Nothing in the chapter suggests a shorter period such as a month; the flood account later dates events by year, month, and day within Noah’s life using the same word.

verses.bibleText: And Enos lived ninety years, and begat Cainan:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Enos lived ninety years, and begat Cainan.” The Hebrew form of the name is Qenan, which sounds like Cain. Several names in Seth’s line resemble names in Cain’s line, and two are identical, Enoch and Lamech. Some have taken this as evidence that the two lists are variants of one original, but the text itself treats them as separate families. The details attached to the shared names are entirely different, and families in the ancient world often reused names that were current in the wider clan.

The parallel names do serve a purpose. They invite comparison, and the comparison shows two lines with very different characters. Cain’s line moved toward violence and self-assertion; Seth’s line, for all its ordinariness, preserved the worship of God and the hope of the promised Seed. Cainan appears again in 1 Chronicles 1:2 and in Luke’s genealogy of Jesus, a small but real link in the chain that leads to Christ.

wordNotes.term: קֵינָן (Qenan) — Cainan
wordNotes.explanation: The name appears to be related to qayin, the name of Cain, and may carry a similar sense, though its precise meaning is uncertain. The shared sound with a name in the rival line shows that similar names circulated in both branches of Adam’s family, without making the two genealogies one.

verses.bibleText: And Enos lived after he begat Cainan eight hundred and fifteen years, and begat sons and daughters:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Enos lived eight hundred and fifteen years after Cainan’s birth and fathered other children. Nothing more is told of him.

He belongs to the large company of faithful people whose names survive while their deeds are known only to God. Yet his life overlapped the early years of Noah, so the worship that began in his generation could be handed on almost to the generation of the flood. The silence of the record is no verdict on his worth. Malachi speaks of “a book of remembrance” written before the LORD for those who feared Him (Malachi 3:16), and names that human history passes over are kept there.

wordNotes.term: אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ (’acharei holido) — after he begat
wordNotes.explanation: This phrase opens the second span in each entry, the years a patriarch lived after his named son was born. Because the first span and the second are both given, the total can be checked by simple addition, which the next verse supplies.

verses.bibleText: And all the days of Enos were nine hundred and five years: and he died.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all the days of Enos were nine hundred and five years: and he died.” The sameness of the formula is part of its force. Generation after generation, the words barely change. Men were born, raised families, worked the cursed ground, and returned to it. “One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh” (Ecclesiastes 1:4). 

Moses, who preserved this record for Israel, wrote elsewhere that God turns humanity back to dust with the command, “Return, ye children of men” (Psalm 90:3). This chapter shows that command being carried out, one generation at a time. The man whose name meant “mortal man” lived over nine centuries and still proved the meaning of his name.

wordNotes.term: חָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים וּתְשַׁע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה (chamesh shanim utsha‘ me’ot shanah) — nine hundred and five years
wordNotes.explanation: The Hebrew literally reads “five years and nine hundred years,” naming the smaller unit first, as is common in these lists. Each unit is counted separately with the word “year” attached, a careful style of reckoning that suits a record meant to preserve exact ages.

verses.bibleText: And Cainan lived seventy years, and begat Mahalaleel:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Cainan lived seventy years, and begat Mahalaleel.” The ages at which these men fathered the named son vary widely, from sixty-five to one hundred and eighty-seven. The variation argues against any artificial scheme. The writer is recording what was preserved, not producing a neat pattern.

The name Mahalaleel most likely means “praise of God,” and it is the only name in the list that openly contains the divine name El. Whatever the parents intended by it, the name fits a family that had begun to call upon the LORD. In a world where Cain’s descendants named a city after their own son (4:17), Cainan gave his son a name that pointed upward.

wordNotes.term: וַיְחִי (vayechi) — and lived
wordNotes.explanation: The ordinary verb for being alive opens nearly every entry: a man “lived” so many years. Its steady repetition makes the change in Enoch’s entry stand out, where “walked with God” takes its place. The writer uses the plain verb to describe ordinary existence before showing what a life lived in fellowship with God looks like.

verses.bibleText: And Cainan lived after he begat Mahalaleel eight hundred and forty years, and begat sons and daughters:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Cainan lived eight hundred and forty years after Mahalaleel was born, the longest such span in the chapter, and he too fathered sons and daughters. The family tree was spreading wide.

The figures mean that three, four, and even more generations lived side by side for centuries. Cainan’s grandchildren and great-grandchildren could learn from him directly, and what the elders modeled shaped the households around them. Each new household was another opportunity for the knowledge of God to be taught, or forgotten. Long life magnified influence, whether toward faithfulness or toward neglect.

wordNotes.term: Καϊνάν (Kainan) — Cainan in Luke
wordNotes.explanation: Luke’s genealogy of Jesus gives the name in this Greek form, following the Greek Old Testament, and places him between Enos and Maleleel exactly as Genesis does. The Hebrew Qenan and the Greek Kainan refer to the same man, a link in the line from Adam to Christ.

verses.bibleText: And all the days of Cainan were nine hundred and ten years: and he died.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all the days of Cainan were nine hundred and ten years: and he died.” Cainan is the fourth in the line to die. By the reckoning of the chapter, Adam, Seth, and Enos had all gone before him. 

Life spans of nine centuries were still the rule, yet not one of them escaped the end. The repeated summary, “all the days,” measures each life as a completed sum, closed and finished, awaiting nothing more in this world.

wordNotes.term: כָּל־יְמֵי (kol-yemei) — all the days of
wordNotes.explanation: Each entry totals a man’s life with this phrase before stating his death. Hebrew often measures a life in days rather than years, a habit that keeps its brevity in view even when the years are many. Moses prays for the wisdom to “number our days,” and Job speaks of a person’s days as fixed by God.

verses.bibleText: And Mahalaleel lived sixty and five years, and begat Jared:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Mahalaleel lived sixty and five years, and begat Jared.” Sixty-five is the youngest age at fatherhood in the chapter, matched only by Enoch in verse 21. The list gives no reason for these differences; it simply records them, which is what one expects of a family register handed down with care.

The meaning of Jared, Yered in Hebrew, is uncertain. It resembles the verb “to go down” or “descend,” and some have read it as a hint of humanity’s decline or as a prayer that God would come down to help. Such readings remain guesses, and the chapter does not invite us to build on them. What is certain is that Jared became the father of Enoch, and that the man who would walk with God grew up in his household. The faithfulness of a son is often the harvest of what was sown in an unremarkable home.

wordNotes.term: יֶרֶד (Yered) — Jared
wordNotes.explanation: The name looks like a form related to yarad, “to go down,” but names in this list are not explained by the text, and their meanings are often disputed. It is wiser to treat Jared’s name as a marker of a real person in the line than as a coded message. Luke records it in the Greek form Iaret.

verses.bibleText: And Mahalaleel lived after he begat Jared eight hundred and thirty years, and begat sons and daughters:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Mahalaleel lived eight hundred and thirty years after Jared’s birth and had other sons and daughters. The man whose name honored God lived through most of the period before the flood, a long testimony in a family that was steadily growing in number.

Those years also meant that Mahalaleel lived to see his grandson Enoch begin to walk with God and, three centuries later, saw him taken. A grandfather whose name honored God had the joy of watching the third generation of his house set apart for fellowship with the Lord.

wordNotes.term: וּבָנוֹת (uvanot) — and daughters
wordNotes.explanation: The daughters in these households are never named, yet the chapter mentions them in every generation. Their presence makes the growth of the family possible and leads directly into 6:1–2, where the multiplying of daughters forms the setting for the fatal mixing of the faithful with the ungodly.

verses.bibleText: And all the days of Mahalaleel were eight hundred ninety and five years: and he died.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all the days of Mahalaleel were eight hundred ninety and five years: and he died.” A man named for the praise of God still came to the end common to all. His death is recorded in the same words as the rest. 

The name that honored God did not shield him from mortality, but it did point to the One in whom the faithful placed their hope beyond the grave: “The dead praise not the LORD… But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and for evermore” (Psalm 115:17–18).

wordNotes.term: מַהֲלַלְאֵל (Mahalal’el) — Mahalaleel
wordNotes.explanation: The name combines a form of halal, “to praise,” the root behind “hallelujah,” with ’el, God. It most likely means “praise of God” or “God is praised.” The same name was borne centuries later by a man of Judah who returned to Jerusalem after the exile.

verses.bibleText: And Jared lived an hundred sixty and two years, and he begat Enoch:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jared lived an hundred sixty and two years, and he begat Enoch.” After several generations of fathers in their sixties to nineties, Jared waits until one hundred and sixty-two. The record gives no explanation; it only prepares, by this small change, for the most remarkable entry in the chapter.

Enoch is the seventh from Adam, a position Jude names directly: “Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied” (Jude 1:14). The seventh place matters because Cain’s line also has a notable seventh generation, Lamech, who took two wives and boasted of killing a man (4:19–24). The two sevenths stand as opposites. In one line, the seventh generation celebrates vengeance; in the other, it walks with God. The comparison shows where each way of life leads.

The name Enoch also appears in Cain’s line, where Cain named a city after his son (4:17). The first Enoch had a city as his monument. The second needed none, for God Himself took him.

wordNotes.term: חֲנוֹךְ (Chanokh) — Enoch
wordNotes.explanation: The name is related to the verb chanakh, used of dedicating a house and of training a child in the way he should go. It probably carries the sense “dedicated” or “initiated.” The same name in Cain’s line was attached to a city, while in Seth’s line it belonged to a man whose life was devoted to God.

verses.bibleText: And Jared lived after he begat Enoch eight hundred years, and begat sons and daughters:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jared lived eight hundred years after Enoch’s birth and had other children. Those years mean that Jared was still alive when his son was taken. He watched the son he had raised disappear from the earth without dying, and he lived on for more than four centuries afterward. 

Few fathers have had such a witness to what God can do with a life given wholly to Him. Every year that Jared lived after that day, the absence of his son was a reminder that death was not the only way a life could end.

Jared’s experience is a small picture of what the faithful in every age are given: evidence that God keeps His promises, set within lives that must still be lived by faith in what has not yet been seen (Hebrews 11:1).

wordNotes.term: שְׁמֹנֶה מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה (shemoneh me’ot shanah) — eight hundred years
wordNotes.explanation: A round figure, the same span given for Adam after Seth’s birth. Round numbers appear among the exact ones in the chapter without any sign that they are symbolic; ancient records often preserved some ages in round terms and others precisely.

verses.bibleText: And all the days of Jared were nine hundred sixty and two years: and he died.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all the days of Jared were nine hundred sixty and two years: and he died.” Jared’s is the second-longest life recorded in Scripture, surpassed only by his grandson Methuselah. Yet the length of his life only sharpens the contrast with his son. Enoch lived on earth a little over a third as long and never died; Jared lived nearly a millennium and went down to the dust. Long life was a mercy in that age, but it was not the highest gift God could give. Being taken into His presence was greater.

The refrain therefore lands differently here. Death was the rule even for a father who had seen its exception in his own son.

wordNotes.term: וַיָּמֹת יֶרֶד (vayyamot Yered) — and Jared died
wordNotes.explanation: The same verb that closes the other entries stands at the end of Jared’s life. Placed just before the account of Enoch, where the verb is conspicuously missing, it heightens the contrast between the normal fate of Adam’s descendants and the unique end of the seventh generation.

verses.bibleText: And Enoch lived sixty and five years, and begat Methuselah:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Enoch lived sixty and five years, and begat Methuselah.” Enoch’s entry begins in the usual way, with the verb “lived” and the birth of a son. From the next verse the pattern bends, and the reason given for the change is tied to this birth: Enoch walked with God “after he begat Methuselah.”

The meaning of Methuselah’s name is uncertain. Proposals include “man of the spear” and “man of sending forth.” A popular interpretation claims that the name means “when he dies, it shall be sent,” as though the flood were announced in it. That reading cannot be established from the Hebrew, and the text gives no such explanation. What the chronology does show, by adding the figures, is that Methuselah died in the very year the flood came. Whether or not his name foretold it, his life spanned the whole period in which God’s patience waited for that generation to repent (1 Peter 3:20).

The son of the man who did not die became the man who lived longest. In one family Scripture shows both the shortest stay on earth and the longest, and neither was outside God’s purpose.

wordNotes.term: מְתוּשֶׁלַח (Metushelach) — Methuselah
wordNotes.explanation: The first part, metu, means “man of.” The second part, shelach, can refer to a missile or weapon or to the act of sending, which yields suggestions such as “man of the dart” or “man of sending.” The meaning is not certain, and theories that read a prophecy of the flood into the name go beyond the evidence.

verses.bibleText: And Enoch walked with God after he begat Methuselah three hundred years, and begat sons and daughters:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Enoch walked with God after he begat Methuselah three hundred years.” Here, for the first time, the formula breaks. Where every other entry says a man “lived,” Enoch’s says he “walked with God.” The writer has found that the ordinary verb of existence does not capture this life. To walk with someone is to share his company, go in his direction, and keep his pace over a long road. The same expression is later used of Noah (6:9), and the idea runs through Scripture as the description of a life in close and continuing fellowship with God (Micah 6:8; Malachi 2:6).

The verb form is the one used of God Himself “walking in the garden in the cool of the day” (3:8). What Adam lost when he hid among the trees, Enoch enjoyed in a fallen world. God had not withdrawn from humanity; He still walked with those who would walk with Him.

The walk is tied to the birth of Methuselah. This need not mean that Enoch had been godless before; he grew up in the faithful line and in a home where the LORD was worshiped. But something in becoming a father appears to have drawn him into a deeper dependence on God. Many parents know how the weight of a child’s life presses them toward prayer. Enoch’s faith took on a new steadiness, and it lasted three hundred years. That length of faithfulness speaks to anyone who finds it hard to walk with God for a single day.

“And begat sons and daughters.” The closest walk with God recorded before the flood was lived inside marriage and family life. Enoch did not withdraw from the world to find holiness. He raised children, worked, and, according to Jude, warned his contemporaries of the Lord’s coming judgment (Jude 1:14–15). Holiness was not a retreat from ordinary duties; it was the way he carried them out. Hebrews explains what made such a walk possible: Enoch “pleased God,” and “without faith it is impossible to please him” (Hebrews 11:5–6).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ חֲנוֹךְ אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים (vayyithallekh Chanokh ’et-ha’elohim) — and Enoch walked with God
wordNotes.explanation: The verb is the reflexive-intensive form of halakh, “to walk,” suggesting walking about, going to and fro, an ongoing manner of life. With the preposition ’et, “with,” it pictures companionship rather than the servant’s posture of walking “before” a master (17:1). The article on “the God” marks the true God in contrast to any rival. The Greek translation renders the phrase “Enoch pleased God,” which Hebrews 11:5 follows.

verses.bibleText: And all the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty and five years:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty and five years.” The total formula appears as usual, but the closing words do not. Every other completed entry in the chapter ends with “and he died.” Enoch’s ends with a number and nothing more. The silence is the first signal of what the next verse will say outright.

Three hundred and sixty-five years made Enoch’s time on earth by far the shortest in the list, less than half that of any other patriarch. By the measure of that age he was taken young. Yet the shortness was not a judgment. The man who lived most closely with God left earth soonest, which shows that a long life, valued as it was, was not the greatest blessing God could bestow. Psalm 73 voices the same hope: “Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory” (Psalm 73:24).

The number matches the days of a solar year, and readers have long noticed it. The text makes nothing of the coincidence, and it should not be turned into a symbol of sun worship or astronomical lore. The point the chapter makes is simpler and more important: here is a life that was complete without being ended by death.

The chronology adds a further detail. Enoch was taken fifty-seven years after Adam died. The first man’s death had confirmed God’s sentence on sin; the translation of the seventh from Adam, not long afterward, gave the faithful a living demonstration that the sentence was not God’s final word.

wordNotes.term: שָׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וְשִׁשִּׁים וְחָמֵשׁ (shalosh me’ot shanah veshishshim vechamesh) — three hundred sixty and five years
wordNotes.explanation: The total is given in the same form as the other entries, but without the verb of death that normally follows. The figure equals the number of days in a solar year; the text draws no lesson from that, and it is safest to read it simply as the length of Enoch’s life on earth.

verses.bibleText: And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.” The repetition of “walked with God” makes it the summary of his whole life, and it explains the ending. Where every other paragraph says “and he died,” this one says “he was not”: he was no longer to be found on earth. The reason is given at once: “for God took him.” Hebrews interprets the event without ambiguity: “By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him” (Hebrews 11:5). He did not die and he was not buried. God removed him, living, from the earth into His presence.

The verb “took” is the one used of Elijah, whom the LORD “would take up… into heaven by a whirlwind” (2 Kings 2:1, 3, 5). Apart from these two, the Old Testament records no one taken from the earth without dying. Enoch’s translation is therefore an exception, and it proves the rule of the chapter: all others who died went to the dust and await the resurrection. The phrase “God took him” is sometimes used today as a gentle way of speaking about a death, but in this text it means the opposite. Enoch was taken precisely so that he would not die.

The event carried a message for the world before the flood and carries one still. Death had reigned without interruption for six generations. Now God showed, in the seventh, that He was able to overrule it and that a life of fellowship with Him leads not to the grave but to His presence. Jude preserves a prophecy of Enoch: “Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, to execute judgment upon all” (Jude 1:14–15). The man who announced the Lord’s coming was himself a preview of what that coming will mean for the faithful.

At Christ’s visible return, believers who have died will be raised, and those still living “shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air” (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51). Enoch is the pledge of that promise, a man who passed from earth to heaven without tasting death. His story assures every believer who walks with God in an evil age that the walk ends at God’s side.

wordNotes.term: וְאֵינֶנּוּ (ve’enennu) — and he was not
wordNotes.explanation: The word combines the particle of nonexistence with a pronoun: “he was no longer there.” It describes absence from a place, not the end of existence; Jacob uses it of Joseph, whom he believed lost but who was alive in Egypt. The Greek translation adds the sense “he was not found,” which Hebrews 11:5 adopts.

wordNotes.term: כִּי־לָקַח אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים (ki-laqach ’oto ’elohim) — for God took him
wordNotes.explanation: Laqach is the common verb “to take,” but with God as subject and a living person as object it describes removal into God’s presence. The same verb is used repeatedly in the account of Elijah’s ascent and appears in the psalmist’s hope that God will “receive” him. The Greek translation renders it metethēken, “transferred” or “translated,” the term Hebrews uses.

verses.bibleText: And Methuselah lived an hundred eighty and seven years, and begat Lamech:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Methuselah lived an hundred eighty and seven years, and begat Lamech.” After Enoch’s extraordinary ending, the formula resumes as though nothing had happened, and life in the family goes on. Methuselah fathers the named son at one hundred and eighty-seven, the oldest age at fatherhood so far.

The son is called Lamech, the same name as the seventh in Cain’s line. The repetition is not careless. Cain’s Lamech took two wives, killed a young man, and turned his violence into a song of boasting, claiming vengeance “seventy and sevenfold” (4:23–24). Seth’s Lamech will speak only once in Scripture, and his words will be a prayerful hope that God will bring relief from the curse (5:29). Two men bear one name and stand for two opposite responses to life in a fallen world: self-assertion that trusts in its own strength, and longing that looks to God.

Lamech was the grandson of Enoch. He was a young man of one hundred and thirteen when his grandfather was taken, old enough to remember it well, and his later hope for comfort may owe something to that memory.

wordNotes.term: לֶמֶךְ (Lemekh) — Lamech
wordNotes.explanation: The meaning of the name is unknown; it has no clear Hebrew root. It is borne by two different men, one in Cain’s line and one in Seth’s, who are distinguished by their place in the genealogy, their families, and above all their words.

verses.bibleText: And Methuselah lived after he begat Lamech seven hundred eighty and two years, and begat sons and daughters:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Methuselah lived seven hundred and eighty-two years after Lamech’s birth and fathered sons and daughters. Those other children, and their families, are part of a sobering silence. When the flood came, only eight persons entered the ark (1 Peter 3:20). Noah’s uncles, aunts, brothers, sisters, and cousins, members of the line that had once called on the name of the LORD, were not among them. 

Belonging to a godly family did not secure anyone’s salvation. Faith may be taught in a home, but each person must receive it for himself (Ezekiel 18:20). Methuselah’s many descendants grew up beside Noah and heard his warnings, and still chose the world that was perishing.

wordNotes.term: וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת (vayyoled banim uvanot) — and begat sons and daughters
wordNotes.explanation: The recurring phrase signals a large extended family in each generation. In the closing generations before the flood it takes on a solemn edge, since none of these unnamed relatives appears among those saved with Noah.

verses.bibleText: And all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years: and he died.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years: and he died.” Methuselah lived longer than anyone else recorded in Scripture. Adding the ages in the chapter places his death in the year of the flood. The text does not say whether he died before the waters came, and it would be unwise to claim more than it says. What is clear is that the oldest man in history lived through the whole period of God’s patience with the antediluvian world and reached its very end.

That patience is the theme Peter draws out: “the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah” (1 Peter 3:20). God gave that generation centuries, and then a final period of one hundred and twenty years (6:3), to turn from violence. Methuselah’s long life stands as a measure of that mercy.

Even so, the longest life falls short of a thousand years. To God, “a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past” (Psalm 90:4). However long a human life stretches, it never approaches the life of the Eternal. The refrain sounds again, the seventh time in the chapter, and it will sound once more for Lamech before the flood sweeps away the world that had grown old in sin.

wordNotes.term: תֵּשַׁע וְשִׁשִּׁים שָׁנָה וּתְשַׁע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה (tesha‘ veshishshim shanah utsha‘ me’ot shanah) — nine hundred sixty and nine years
wordNotes.explanation: The longest lifespan in Scripture is stated in the same plain form as the others, with the smaller units first. Added to the ages at fatherhood in the following verses, it brings Methuselah’s death to the year the flood began, the six hundredth year of Noah’s life.

verses.bibleText: And Lamech lived an hundred eighty and two years, and begat a son:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Lamech lived an hundred eighty and two years, and begat a son.” The verse departs from the pattern in a small way that matters. Every earlier entry names the son in the same breath as his birth. Here the son is introduced without a name, and the naming is held back for a sentence of its own. The pause draws the reader’s attention forward, as though the narrative were taking a breath before announcing the child on whom the story will now turn.

Noah was the first in the line born after Adam’s death. The first man had passed from the scene, and the father of the new world was about to enter it. In the chronology of Genesis, Lamech himself was the last of the line who could have known Adam in person.

wordNotes.term: בֵּן (ben) — a son
wordNotes.explanation: The ordinary word for a son stands here without a name, unlike every other birth in the chapter. The delay sets up the explanation of Noah’s name in the next verse, the only name in the list that is explained.

verses.bibleText: And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he called his name Noah, saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed.” This is the only spoken sentence in the chapter and the only name the chapter explains. Lamech gives voice to what the whole list has been showing: life under the curse is labor and sorrow that ends in death. His words reach straight back to the sentence on Adam: “cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it” (3:17). The word translated “toil” is the same word as that “sorrow.” Lamech felt in his own hands what Adam’s sin had brought.

His words are also the only place in the chapter where the covenant name, “the LORD,” appears. He traces the curse to God, but he also looks to God for relief. The hope that the woman’s Seed would one day undo what the serpent had done (3:15) seems to stand behind his words. He may have hoped that Noah himself would be that deliverer.

The name Noah sounds like the Hebrew for “rest,” while the verb Lamech uses means “to comfort” or “give relief.” The two ideas run through the flood narrative that follows. God “repented” (6:6), from the same root as “comfort”; the ark “rested” on the mountains of Ararat (8:4); and Noah’s sacrifice rose as a “sweet savour,” literally an aroma of rest (8:21). After that sacrifice God promised never again to curse the ground on humanity’s account (8:21). Lamech’s hope was answered, though not in the way he could have imagined, and only after judgment had passed over the earth.

Noah was not the final deliverer. The full answer to Lamech’s longing came in the One who says, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Through Christ the curse itself will be removed: “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3). Until then “there remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), a rest already tasted in fellowship with Him and in the weekly Sabbath that recalls the finished work of creation and points to the restoration still to come.

wordNotes.term: נֹחַ … יְנַחֲמֵנוּ (Noach… yenachamenu) — Noah… shall comfort us
wordNotes.explanation: The name Noach is linked by sound with nuach, “to rest,” while the verb Lamech uses comes from nacham, “to comfort” or “bring relief.” The explanation is a play on sounds rather than a technical etymology, and the two ideas are close enough that Ezekiel sets them in parallel. The same root nacham returns when God “repented” that He had made man, so the comfort Lamech hoped for came through judgment and renewal.

wordNotes.term: עִצְּבוֹן יָדֵינוּ (‘itsevon yadeinu) — toil of our hands
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Itsavon means painful labor or sorrow and occurs only three times in the Old Testament, all in Genesis 3 and 5. God used it in pronouncing judgment on the woman and on the man. Lamech’s use of the rare word shows that he understood his hard labor as the outworking of the curse spoken in Eden.

verses.bibleText: And Lamech lived after he begat Noah five hundred ninety and five years, and begat sons and daughters:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Lamech lived five hundred and ninety-five years after Noah’s birth and had other sons and daughters. He watched his son grow, saw him become a preacher of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5), and may have seen the ark take shape. 

Yet he did not see the flood or the relief he had hoped for. Like the faithful described in Hebrews, he “died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off” (Hebrews 11:13). His hope was not mistaken because he died before seeing it fulfilled; it was simply larger than his own lifetime.

wordNotes.term: אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ אֶת־נֹחַ (’acharei holido ’et-Noach) — after he begat Noah
wordNotes.explanation: The standard phrase for the second span of life gains weight when it names Noah. Lamech’s remaining years were spent in the shadow of the son on whom he had placed his hope, and the phrase measures the long time he waited.

verses.bibleText: And all the days of Lamech were seven hundred seventy and seven years: and he died.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And all the days of Lamech were seven hundred seventy and seven years: and he died.” Lamech died five years before the flood, the shortest life in the chapter apart from Enoch’s. The final death in the list falls on the man who had voiced the chapter’s hope.

The figure seven hundred seventy and seven is striking beside the boast of Cain’s Lamech, who claimed vengeance “seventy and sevenfold” (4:24). The text does not comment on the echo, and it should not be pressed. Yet the contrast between the two Lamechs is real. One measured his life by the revenge he could take; the other is remembered for the comfort he sought from God. Jesus would later turn the boast of vengeance upside down, calling His followers to forgive “until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22).

wordNotes.term: שֶׁבַע וְשִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה וּשְׁבַע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה (sheva‘ veshiv‘im shanah ushva‘ me’ot shanah) — seven hundred seventy and seven years
wordNotes.explanation: The number repeats the digit seven three times. It is recorded as a plain lifespan, but it sits within a passage where seven carries weight: Enoch is the seventh from Adam, and Cain’s Lamech boasted of seventy-sevenfold vengeance.

verses.bibleText: And Noah was five hundred years old: and Noah begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Noah was five hundred years old: and Noah begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” The genealogy reaches its tenth generation and changes shape. Instead of one named son followed by “sons and daughters,” three sons are named together, and no further years or death are recorded. Noah’s entry is left open. Its conclusion comes only in 9:28–29, after the flood, so that the whole flood narrative is set within the record of his life.

The Hebrew reads literally that Noah was “a son of five hundred years,” an idiom meaning that he was in that year of his life. The verse does not claim that all three sons were born at once. Comparison with other passages shows that they were born over a period of years. Shem was one hundred years old two years after the flood (11:10), which places his birth in Noah’s five hundred and second year. Ham is called the youngest (9:24), and the King James rendering of 10:21 identifies Japheth as “the elder.” The oldest son, Japheth, was likely born when Noah was five hundred, and the others followed.

Shem is named first because of his importance, not his age. Through him the line of promise continues (11:10–26), down to Abraham and eventually to Christ (Luke 3:36). Genesis often lists sons in order of significance for the story it is telling, as it later lists Abram first among Terah’s sons.

Noah waited five centuries before fathering children, far longer than any of his ancestors. The delay may reflect God’s providence: the sons who would enter the ark with him were born close to the time of the flood. The three names will soon stand for the peoples of the whole earth (10:1, 32). The chapter that began with one man created in God’s likeness ends with the three from whom all later nations come, and with a family through whom God will preserve both the human race and the promise of the Seed.

wordNotes.term: בֶּן־חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה (ben-chamesh me’ot shanah) — five hundred years old
wordNotes.explanation: Hebrew expresses age with the idiom “son of so many years.” The phrase indicates the year of life one is in, as the flood account shows when it dates the same event both as Noah being “six hundred years old” and as occurring “in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life.”

wordNotes.term: שֵׁם חָם וָיָפֶת (Shem, Cham, vaYafet) — Shem, Ham, and Japheth
wordNotes.explanation: The order is not the order of birth. Ham is the youngest, and Shem’s age after the flood shows he was born two years after his eldest brother. Shem comes first because the line of promise runs through him; his name means “name,” fitting the son from whose descendants God would make a great name for Abraham.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: If your life were summed up in one line of a family record, what would that line say?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Death reigns over Adam’s race exactly as God warned, yet God keeps the line of promise alive, takes Enoch who walked with Him, and kindles hope for rest from the curse.
discussionQuestions: Why does the chapter begin by recalling the creation of humanity in God’s likeness before listing deaths?
What does the repeated refrain “and he died” teach about the reality of sin’s penalty?
How does Enoch’s walk with God compare with the life of the seventh generation in Cain’s line?
What did Lamech hope Noah would bring, and how was that hope answered in ways he could not foresee?
How does Enoch’s translation encourage believers who expect Christ’s return?
commonMisunderstandings: The long ages are not myths or dynasties; the text presents them as real lifespans in real history.
“God took him” does not mean Enoch died; Hebrews 11:5 says he was translated so that he should not see death.
The deaths recorded here do not describe souls departing to live elsewhere; the dead return to dust and await the resurrection.
Enoch’s walk with God did not begin as an escape from family life; he walked with God while raising sons and daughters.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together the somber refrain of death and the bright exceptions of grace: God’s word about sin proved true, and His promise of deliverance proved true as well.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Walk with God today in the ordinary duties of home and work, trusting the One who conquered death and will come again to take His people to Himself.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Death entered through sin and reigns over every descendant of Adam, but God has provided victory over death through Christ, pictured in Enoch’s translation and completed at the Second Coming.
flow: God made humanity in His likeness and blessed it.
Through sin, death passed to all, and the refrain “and he died” proves God’s warning true.
The dead rest in the dust until the resurrection; Scripture gives no conscious life apart from the body.
Enoch, who walked with God by faith, was taken without dying, a pledge of what God will do for the living saints at Christ’s return.
Christ, the true Seed, brings the rest and comfort Lamech longed for and calls each person to walk with Him now.
simpleIllustrations: A family Bible with its list of births and deaths shows that every name ends the same way, unless someone outside the family intervenes.
Two friends walking the same road for years come to share the same direction, pace, and destination; Enoch’s walk ended at God’s home.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you begin walking with God through faith in Christ, so that whether you sleep in death or live to see His coming, you will be His?
cautions: Do not set dates or speculate about who will be translated; keep the focus on faithful daily fellowship with God.
Do not treat the long lifespans as a reward that can be earned by diet or discipline alone.
Avoid building doctrine on uncertain meanings of the patriarchs’ names.

reflectionQuestions: When I read “and he died” eight times over, what does it teach me about the seriousness of sin and the faithfulness of God’s word?
In what part of my ordinary family and work life am I being called to walk with God more closely?
Do I live with the hope that Christ’s coming will end death’s reign, or have I settled into the routine of birth, labor, and death?
What “toil of my hands” makes me long, like Lamech, for the rest that only God can give?
How can I pass on to the next generation what I have learned about God, as Adam could to his descendants?
